newsitem.title: USA: U.S. taps Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary for NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. taps Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary for NATO.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday that it favours only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join NATO in the first round of new members to be invited to enter the security alliance.

The decision, formally presented by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen at a NATO defence ministers meeting in Brussels, flies in the face of an effort by France and others to include Romania and Slovenia in the first wave.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the United States' stance was firm, that it would work to achieve consensus on the issue before the NATO summit in Madrid that will formally invite new members to begin membership negotiations, and that it did not expect to be overruled by its allies.

"The United States will formally say today that of the candidate members for admission to NATO we will favour in the first round Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary as the nations at this point most ready economically, politically and militarily to take on the enormous responsibilities of being members of our most important strategic alliance," he said.

"There obviously were other serious candidates -- Romania and Slovenia both are clearly on track -- but in the view of the United States they will profit by having more time to fully develop their capacities within the parameters of the Partnership for Peace Programme," McCurry told reporters.

"We do continue to favour an open-door policy with respect to NATO membership and no one should be excluded from consideration and this should not be considered the last round of admissions," he added.
Expanding the 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) has been studied since 1994, but had been steadfastly opposed by Russia until this spring.

The alliance paved the way to its eastward expansion last month when President Bill Clinton, Russian President Boris Yeltsin and the other alliance members signed the "NATO-Russia Founding Act" to chart their future relations.

The new members are to be invited to begin negotiations to join the alliance at a July 8-9 Madrid summit, possibly with the aim of their actually becoming members in 1999, the 50th anniversary of NATO's founding.
McCurry told reporters that the decision for the United States to favour only the three to join NATO in the first round reflected a mix of economic, political and military factors.

"The United States evaluated this issue, looking at those countries that had the highest standards in terms of their own military capaicity (as well as) the status of their political and economic reforms, because that is an aspect of the ability to carry out responsibilities in the alliance," he said.
"Our own military believes that NATO will better be able to absorb new members if we start with three, so there was a military reason to keep the number at three," he added.

McCurry suggested that the United States would not budge from its position on admitting only the three countries and that it did not expect to be overruled within NATO's decision-making North Atlantic Council.
"The United States position is firm," McCurry said. Asked if the United States might be overruled on the matter by other NATO members, he replied: "That's not likely."
Asked if he expected a fight at Madrid, when the formal invitations will be issued, he replied: "No, we expect the celebration of three new members of the alliance."
U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott met with ambassadors from the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland on Thursday to tell them formally of the U.S. decision.
Hungarian charge d'affaires Gabor Horvath told reporters after the meeting that he was delighted by the decision.

"We were very pleased. It's a historic moment," he said. "The vision of having a unified, peaceful and stable Europe is making another very strong step. And it is also very important the process should and will remain open for making this Europe broader, even more stable, even more unified for the future."
Talbott was expected to meet separately with ambassadors from Romania and Slovenia to explain the U.S. decision.
